evidence.claim: The Millen-Jenkins County Scenic Byway makes a 35-mile loop from downtown Millen through woodland, pasture and scattered farm communities.
evidence.quote: This 35-mile Scenic Byway begins in the Downtown Millen Historic District.

evidence.claim: Georgia DOT includes it among the state’s designated scenic byways, highlighting historic farmhouses, churches and the open farmland along SR 17.
evidence.quote: There are 17​ corridors that have achieved Georgia Scenic Byways status as designated by the Georgia DOT.

evidence.claim: On SR 23 and Perkins Green Fork Road, woods and pasture share the route with old farmhouses; Herndon Road brings historic churches into the drive.
evidence.quote: Proceeding to SR 23 and Perkins Green Fork Road, scenic character is exhibited by woodlands, pasturelands, and historic farmhouses in small and scattered communities. Varied and distinctive viewsheds are found on Herndon Road, along with several historic churches.

evidence.claim: The loop’s starting point grew at a railroad connection: in 1854, the Central of Georgia Railway and the Georgia Railroad met at the settlement then called 79.
evidence.quote: In 1854, the Central of Georgia Railway and the Georgia Railroad connected at 79.

evidence.claim: The town became Millen’s Junction, taking the name of Central of Georgia superintendent McPherson B. Millen.
evidence.quote: The town became known as "Millen's Junction" after McPherson B. Millen, the superintendent of the Central of Georgia Railway.

evidence.claim: Union soldiers destroyed the junction during the Civil War, and the town was rebuilt afterward.
evidence.quote:
The Union soldiers destroyed Millen's Junction after finding the prison camp and to avoid use of the railway junction.
The town was rebuilt after the war.

evidence.claim: The downtown depots date from the early 1900s.
evidence.quote: Its railroad depots date from the early 1900s.

evidence.claim: Begin in the Downtown Millen Historic District, follow SR 23 and Perkins Green Fork Road toward the loop’s northern reach, then continue by Herndon Road and return on SR 17 to Cotton Avenue.
evidence.quote: SR 17, heading back to Cotton Avenue, is characterized simply by wide-open farmland stretching for miles.

evidence.claim: Near Perkins, Big Buckhead Church Road marks the loop’s northernmost point.
evidence.quote: Head south on US 25 to Big Buckhead Church Road (near the town of Perkins). Turn either way on Big Buckhead Church Road. The byway is a loop, and this is its northernmost point.

evidence.claim: Magnolia Springs State Park is a separate excursion, three miles from the SR 17 and US 25 intersection.
evidence.quote: Magnolia Springs State Park is located three miles from the intersection of SR 17 and US 25.

evidence.claim: Union soldiers destroyed the railway junction in 1864; the town was rebuilt after the war.
evidence.quote: On December 3, 1864, Sherman's March to the Sea passed through Millen.

evidence.claim: In 1905, Millen became the seat of newly created Jenkins County.
evidence.quote: becoming the county seat of the newly created Jenkins County in 1905.

evidence.claim: The county courthouse followed in 1910, designed by L.F. Goodrich in the Neoclassical Revival style.
evidence.quote: Designed in a Neoclassical Revival architecture style by L.F. Goodrich, it was built in 1910.

evidence.claim: Its three stories rise to a copper-domed clock tower, with plain and fluted columns set on high bases.
evidence.quote: Unlike most courthouses in Georgia of the period, this one is three stories tall.  It has columns that are plain and fluted, which are on high bases.  The building has a bracketed cornice.  On top is a copper-domed clock tower.

evidence.claim: Carswell Grove’s congregation meets in a building constructed in 2008 beside the site of its lost historic church.
evidence.quote: the congregation meets in a more modest and modern adjacent building built in 2008.

evidence.claim: After emancipation, Black worshippers who had occupied segregated pews at nearby Big Buckhead Baptist Church formed a separate congregation on land given by Porter W. Carswell.
evidence.quote: White judge Porter W. Carswell gave blacks 2 acres (0.81 ha) nearby to build their own church; they named it in his honor.

evidence.claim: Their original church was the first of seven Black churches burned during the Jenkins County violence of 1919.
evidence.quote: The original church was the first of seven black churches burned in the Jenkins County, Georgia, riot of 1919.

evidence.claim: A replacement built that year was itself destroyed by arson in 2014.
evidence.quote: The church, a replacement for an earlier church burned in 1919, was destroyed by arson in 2014.

evidence.claim: Black worshippers who had occupied segregated pews at nearby Big Buckhead Baptist Church
evidence.quote: Prior to the Civil War blacks had worshipped there in segregated pews;

evidence.claim: Magnolia Springs supplied water for Camp Lawton, a Confederate prison for Union soldiers established in 1864.
evidence.quote: Camp Lawton was established during the Civil War in the fall of 1864 by the Confederate Army to house Union prisoners of war. The Magnolia Springs site was selected to take advantage of the abundant water supply.

evidence.claim: Enslaved laborers and Union prisoners built the stockade from pine cut on the site.
evidence.quote: Built by slave labor and a group of Union prisoners of pine timber harvested on site

evidence.claim: It opened in October and was evacuated within six weeks as Sherman’s army advanced.
evidence.quote: It opened in October 1864 but had to be evacuated within six weeks, due to the advance of Sherman's army through Georgia.

evidence.claim: Little of the stockade remains, but the earthen breastworks are visible.
evidence.quote: Today, little remains of the prison stockade; however, the earthen breastworks which guarded it may still be seen.

evidence.claim: Archaeologists uncovered the stockade wall and soldiers’ personal articles in 2010; artifacts are displayed in the park’s Camp Lawton museum.
evidence.quote: During 2010, Georgia Southern University archeology teams uncovered the stockade wall and numerous personal articles from soldiers.

evidence.claim: A boardwalk crosses the spring water; the prison’s earthen breastworks remain visible.
evidence.quote: A boardwalk spans the cool water, allowing visitors to look for alligators, turtles and other wildlife near the springs.

evidence.claim: artifacts are displayed in the park’s Camp Lawton museum.
evidence.quote: Artifacts are currently on display at the university and at the Camp Lawton museum located at Magnolia Springs State Park.

evidence.claim: The nearby railroad and drinking water from Magnolia Springs also made the area a site for a Confederate prison.
evidence.quote: It was built in what is today Magnolia Springs State Park, because the location was favorable due to the springs providing potable water and its proximity to the Augusta and Savannah Railroad.

evidence.claim: Downtown Millen’s railroad depots date from the early 1900s.
evidence.quote: Its railroad depots date from the early 1900s.

evidence.claim: The downtown historic district entered the National Register in 1996, when its inventory included 44 contributing buildings, four structures and two objects.
evidence.quote: which was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1996.  It then included 44 contributing buildings, four contributing structures, and two contributing objects.

evidence.claim: The cemetery dates to around 1870, when the first church was built, and extends along the church site’s rear and sides.
evidence.quote: The cemetery was founded around 1870, when the original church building was built.  It is located along the rear and sides of the church

evidence.claim: The spring flows seven million gallons a day, and a boardwalk spans the water where visitors can look for turtles and alligators.
evidence.quote: Beautiful Magnolia Springs State Park is known for its crystal clear springs flowing 7 million gallons per day. A boardwalk spans the cool water, allowing visitors to look for alligators, turtles and other wildlife near the springs.

flags: The cache documents the landscape and route but not the construction or designation history of the constituent roads; the historical paragraph therefore follows the starting town’s railroad history.
GDOT gives 35 miles; material has 40.1 mapped miles. Used the cached official mileage.
Loop order begins downtown, passes Carswell Grove near the northern reach and places the Magnolia Springs excursion with the return toward Millen.

The official park page reports a lake boating closure. No boating is proposed here; the closure does not establish a road closure. GDOT’s aquarium reference conflicts with the cached park history saying it closed in 2010; omitted aquarium.
Carswell Grove history lacks a cached congregation or archival source; no access or surviving historic church is promised.
